content: Amniotomy, also referred to as the artificial rupture of the amniotic membranes or breaking of the waters, is a widely practiced procedure in modern obstetrics and midwifery. Its primary purpose is to accelerate uterine contractions and thereby reduce the duration of labor. However, there are concerns about potential unintended adverse effects on both the mother and the baby. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of amniotomy as a standalone intervention for routinely shortening labor that begins spontaneously. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing amniotomy alone to the intention of preserving the membranes. Quasi-randomized trials were excluded from the analysis. The review incorporated data from 15 studies involving a total of 5,583 women. When comparing amniotomy alone to the preservation of membranes during spontaneous labor, the findings showed no statistically significant difference in the duration of the first stage of labor. The mean difference was -20.43 minutes, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from -95.93 to 55.06 minutes. Similarly, there was no significant difference in the rate of cesarean sections (risk ratio 1.27, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.63), maternal satisfaction with the childbirth experience (mean difference -1.10, 95% CI -7.15 to 4.95), or the likelihood of an Apgar score below seven at five minutes (risk ratio 0.53, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.00). Additionally, the timing of amniotomy during labor, in terms of cervical dilation, varied across the included trials. For cases of spontaneous labor that had become prolonged, the comparison between amniotomy and the preservation of membranes also revealed no statistically significant differences. The rate of cesarean sections (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.15 to 6.08), maternal satisfaction with the childbirth experience (mean difference 22.00, 95% CI 2.74 to 41.26), and the likelihood of an Apgar score below seven at five minutes (risk ratio 2.86, 95% CI 0.12 to 66.11) were all comparable between the two groups. Based on the findings of this review, there is insufficient evidence to recommend the routine use of amniotomy as part of standard labor management and care. The evidence presented in this review should be shared with women who are offered an amniotomy, as it may serve as a valuable basis for informed discussions and decision-making between women and their healthcare providers.
